## Five kinds of information in one picture

A printed melody hands you pitch, time, grouping, spelling, and expression in
one compact image. Take all five at once and your errors stop being locatable. You can copy every pitch correctly and still end up with a bar that's
half a beat short.

So decode in a fixed order: time signature, key signature, rhythm, pitches,
ties, then articulation. Each pass enriches the same score data and leaves
evidence you can inspect. Structure first means every bar already holds its
promised time, and every accidental already has a definite effect, before sound
design gets a vote.

## The four bars, in characters

```text
Treble clef.  4/4.  Key signature: one sharp (F).

       |   bar 1    |     bar 2     |     bar 3     |  bar 4  |
 10 F5 |------------|---------------|---------------|---------|
  9 E5 |            |               |               |         |
  8 D5 |---------D--|---------------|D--------------|---------|
  7 C5 |            |C              |   C           |         |
  6 B4 |------B-----|---B-----------|------B--------|---------|
  5 A4 |   A        |      A        |         A     |   A     |
  4 G4 |G-----------|---------G~-G--|---------------|G-----G--|
  3 F4 |            |               |            F  |         |
  2 E4 |------------|---------------|---------------|---------|
beats  |1  1  1  1  |.5 .5 1  1~ 1  |1  1  .5 .5 1  |1  1  2  |
```

Engraved staff figures are still to come. Treat the sketch above as scaffolding,
never as a substitute for real notation.

Each gutter row is one staff line or space, labelled with its [Lesson 38](38-treble-clef-coordinate-system.qmd)
coordinate and the letter and octave it names. Note heads are letters in their
own row. The bottom row gives each note's length in beats; `~` marks a tie.

Decode it yourself before scrolling, as pitch and duration pairs. Two things
need a decision. Bar three's F carries no sign, and the signature has something
to say about it. Bar two ties two one-beat Gs: five attacks, or four?

## The same bars, already decoded

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92
use_synth :piano

# Four bars in 4/4, already resolved from a one-sharp key signature.
bars = [
  [[:g4, 1], [:a4, 1], [:b4, 1], [:d5, 1]],
  [[:c5, 0.5], [:b4, 0.5], [:a4, 1], [:g4, 2]],
  [[:d5, 1], [:c5, 1], [:b4, 0.5], [:a4, 0.5], [:fs4, 1]],
  [[:g4, 1], [:a4, 1], [:g4, 2]]
]

bars.each_with_index do |bar, index|
  total = bar.sum { |pitch, duration| duration }
  raise "bar #{index + 1} totals #{total}" unless total == 4
end

score = []
cursor = 0
bars.each do |bar|
  bar.each do |pitch, duration|
    score << {note: pitch, start: cursor, duration: duration}
    cursor += duration
  end
end

define :play_events do |events|
  cursor = 0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note], sustain: event[:duration] * 0.82,
      release: 0.08
    sleep event[:duration]
    cursor = event[:start] + event[:duration]
  end
end

puts "#{score.length} events, #{cursor} beats"
play_events score
```

Check your answer against that array. Bar two holds four events: the tie merged
two written one-beat Gs into one sounding note of two beats. Bar three's F
arrives as `:fs4`, the signature's default made explicit. Every bar total is
verified before a sound is scheduled, so no question of spelling or length is
still hiding in the renderer.

## Three ways to break it

1. Change bar three's last duration from `1` to `0.5`. The check halts the
   program before playback, so a metric defect can't disguise itself as a tempo
   problem.
2. Split bar two's final G into two one-beat events. The total is still four and
   the check still passes, but you'll hear a second attack. Bar arithmetic and
   tie reading are different validations; only one is automatic.
3. Restore the score, then change synth and release. Timbre reshapes clarity
   while pitches and timings sit there unchanged.

## What each pass can actually prove

Every 4/4 bar totals four quarter-note beats. That invariant lets you enter and
check rhythm before you know a single pitch. Key resolution then combines source
spelling with signature defaults. Ties merge adjacent written durations into one
event, and articulation stays a rendering choice. Each stage answers a narrower
question than "read the music."

Nested bars keep the measure boundaries you can see on the page. The flattened score is renderer-facing, with absolute starts.
Both come from the same arrays, so there's no second hand-typed transcription to
drift, and any doubtful event traces back to its measure.

Listening is another validation pass, not a reward at the end. Loop a suspicious bar
against a lawful source recording where one exists. A correct bar total never
catches a wrong pitch. Valid Ruby never catches a wrong rhythm that adds
up to four. Assertions shrink the search space; your ears and the page do the
rest.

Provenance belongs beside the score data. Write down edition, page, system, and
measure, though Sonic Pi will never read them. When a note sounds doubtful,
that pointer takes you back to the evidence. Part 9 grows it into a full source
record: [Lesson 42](../09-transcription/42-finding-music-you-can-legally-use.qmd) adds edition details, rights information, retrieval date, and
a redistribution decision, all expensive to recover once the transcription
outgrows four bars.

## Decode these, then go and find four more

Type the four bars above from the character staff, without looking at the Ruby.
Enter meter and rhythm first, and make every bar-total assertion pass before you
touch pitch. Then add spelling, resolve the signature with your [Lesson 40](40-key-signatures-defaults.qmd)
function, merge the tie, and add articulation last. Note which pass caught each
mistake.

Then do it again with four bars from a public-domain score you chose yourself,
recording the exact edition. Save each pass as its own version, keep source
measure numbers in comments, and render without importing a MIDI file. List
everything still needing comparison against the page or an authorised recording.
Uncertainty you wrote down is cheaper than certainty you invented.
